concepts.name: Weathering vs. Erosion vs. Mass Wasting: Conceptual Boundaries
key_dimensions: Precise definition of weathering as in-situ disintegration/decomposition with NO transport
How erosion differs by involving active agents of transport (water, wind, ice)
Mass wasting as a bridge concept — involves movement but driven by gravity, not a fluid agent
UPSC trap: confusing weathering with denudation (denudation is the broader umbrella term)

concepts.name: Mechanical (Physical) Weathering: Types and Controlling Factors
key_dimensions: Key processes: frost action, insolation weathering, pressure release (unloading), salt crystallization
Role of diurnal temperature range vs. freeze-thaw cycles in different climatic zones
Why mechanical weathering dominates in arid/polar climates (low moisture, extreme temperatures)
UPSC trap: insolation weathering attributed to thermal expansion — debate on whether moisture is also required

concepts.name: Frost Action (Freeze-Thaw Weathering): Mechanism and Landforms
key_dimensions: Mechanism: water expands ~9% on freezing, exerting pressure up to 2,100 kg/cm² in joints
Conditions required: temperature must oscillate around 0°C repeatedly (periglacial zones)
Landforms produced: blockfields (felsenmeer), scree/talus slopes, patterned ground
Distinction between congelifraction (frost shattering) and congeliturbation (frost heaving in soil)

concepts.name: Exfoliation and Pressure Release Weathering: Mechanisms and Debate
key_dimensions: Sheeting/unloading: removal of overlying rock reduces confining pressure, causing expansion and sheet joints
Thermal exfoliation (onion-skin weathering): debated role of pure thermal cycling vs. moisture-assisted expansion
Landforms: exfoliation domes (e.g., Half Dome, Yosemite), bornhardts in tropical regions
UPSC trap: exfoliation domes are often confused as products of chemical weathering; primary mechanism is physical

concepts.name: Salt Crystallization (Haloclasty): Process and Geographic Significance
key_dimensions: Mechanism: salts precipitate in pores/cracks and crystal growth exerts disruptive pressure
Most effective salts: sodium sulfate, sodium carbonate (expand more than halite on hydration)
Dominant in hot deserts, coastal zones, and areas with high evaporation rates
UPSC trap: often overlooked as a major weathering agent; more effective than frost action in arid tropics

concepts.name: Chemical Weathering: Core Processes and Their Interrelationships
key_dimensions: Six key processes: solution, hydration, hydrolysis, oxidation, reduction, carbonation
Role of water and temperature as the two master controls (rate doubles with every 10°C rise — van't Hoff's Law)
Why chemical weathering dominates in humid tropical climates
UPSC trap: hydrolysis vs. hydration — hydration is physical attachment of water molecules; hydrolysis is a chemical reaction breaking mineral bonds

concepts.name: Carbonation: Process, Products, and Karst Significance
key_dimensions: Reaction: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃; H₂CO₃ + CaCO₃ → Ca(HCO₃)₂ (soluble, carried away)
Reversibility: precipitation of CaCO₃ when CO₂ is released forms speleothems (stalactites/stalagmites)
Role in karst topography formation: sinkholes, caves, dolines, uvalas, poljes
UPSC trap: carbonation dissolves limestone but the process itself is chemical, not purely physical solution

concepts.name: Hydrolysis: The Most Important Chemical Weathering Process
key_dimensions: Mechanism: H⁺ and OH⁻ ions from water react with silicate mineral cations, breaking the mineral lattice
Products: clay minerals (kaolinite, illite, smectite) + silicic acid + cations in solution
Feldspars (most abundant mineral) are primary targets: orthoclase → kaolinite + silica + K⁺
UPSC trap: hydrolysis is the primary process forming laterite and bauxite soils in tropics, not oxidation alone

concepts.name: Oxidation and Reduction in Weathering: Contrasting Environments
key_dimensions: Oxidation: addition of oxygen to minerals (especially iron-bearing); produces iron oxides (hematite, limonite) — 'rusting of rocks'
Reduction (gleization): occurs in waterlogged/anaerobic conditions; iron reduced to Fe²⁺ giving grey/blue-green color (gleyed soils)
Role in distinguishing well-drained lateritic profiles (red, oxidized) from waterlogged profiles
UPSC trap: the red color of soils/rocks is due to hematite (Fe₂O₃) from oxidation, NOT due to carbonation or hydrolysis

concepts.name: Biological Weathering: Mechanisms and Underrated Significance
key_dimensions: Physical bio-weathering: root wedging, burrowing organisms (bioturbation), lichens physically disrupting rock
Chemical bio-weathering: organic acids (humic, fulvic, oxalic acids) from decomposing matter and root exudates
Chelation: organic acids form complexes with metal cations, removing them from the mineral structure
UPSC trap: lichens are the PIONEER organisms in rock weathering — they combine physical and chemical attack simultaneously

concepts.name: Factors Controlling the Rate and Type of Weathering
key_dimensions: Climate (temperature + moisture): the overriding control — hot-humid = chemical dominant; cold-arid = physical dominant
Rock characteristics: mineralogy (silica content, mineral stability — Bowen's Reaction Series), texture, jointing, porosity
Relief/topography: slope angle affects water retention and drainage; affects depth of weathering profile
UPSC trap: Bowen's Reaction Series predicts weathering susceptibility — minerals crystallizing LAST (quartz, muscovite) are MOST resistant

concepts.name: Bowen's Reaction Series and Mineral Susceptibility to Weathering
key_dimensions: Goldich's Dissolution Series mirrors Bowen's: olivine/pyroxene weather fastest; quartz weathers slowest
Reasoning: minerals formed at highest temperatures are least stable at Earth's surface conditions
Practical implication: basaltic/mafic rocks weather faster and deeper than granitic/felsic rocks in humid climates
UPSC trap: granite is more resistant to chemical weathering than basalt despite being harder — composition matters more than hardness

concepts.name: Deep Chemical Weathering Profiles: Saprolite, Regolith, and Laterite
key_dimensions: Weathering profile layers from top: soil → laterite/duricrust → mottled zone → pallid zone → saprolite → fresh bedrock
Saprolite: rock weathered in situ but retaining original rock structure (no transport)
Laterization: intense leaching removes silica and bases; residual enrichment of Fe and Al oxides (sesquioxides)
UPSC trap: laterite is a product of BOTH hydrolysis AND oxidation in alternating wet-dry tropical conditions — not just oxidation

concepts.name: Laterite and Bauxite Formation: Processes and Geographic Distribution
key_dimensions: Laterite: iron-rich (ferricrete); Bauxite: aluminum-rich (alucrete) — both are duricrusts formed by differential leaching
Conditions: high rainfall + high temperature + seasonal dry period for capillary rise and precipitation of oxides
Geographic extent: Deccan Plateau (India), West Africa, Amazon Basin — ancient stable cratonic surfaces
UPSC trap: bauxite forms from aluminum-rich parent rocks (e.g., syenite, nepheline syenite) under more intense leaching than laterite

concepts.name: Spheroidal Weathering: Process and Products
key_dimensions: Mechanism: chemical weathering penetrates rock along joint intersections; corners and edges weather faster than faces (more surface area)
Result: angular blocks progressively rounded into spheres — produces 'core stones' surrounded by 'rotten rock' (grus)
Commonly seen in granite and basalt in humid/tropical regions
UPSC trap: spheroidal weathering is a CHEMICAL process (not mechanical) — the rounded boulders in a laterite landscape are core stones, not transported boulders

concepts.name: Tafoni and Honeycomb Weathering (Alveolar Weathering): Arid and Coastal Contexts
key_dimensions: Tafoni: cavernous hollows in rock faces, common in granites in coastal and arid environments
Mechanisms debated: salt crystallization, moisture-driven hydration, wetting-drying cycles
Honeycomb (alveolar) weathering: small pits due to differential salt crystallization in porous rock
UPSC trap: tafoni is NOT a product of wind erosion (aeolian) — it is a weathering feature; wind may enlarge but not initiate it

concepts.name: Differential Weathering: Rock Resistance and Landscape Formation
key_dimensions: Concept: rocks of varying composition/structure weather at different rates, creating relief
Examples: inselbergs/bornhardts (resistant granite cores), hoodoos/earth pillars (harder cap protecting softer rock)
Role in structural landforms: hogbacks, cuestas, mesas, and buttes reflect differential resistance
UPSC trap: inselbergs are products of differential deep weathering (etchplanation theory) — NOT purely erosional remnants

concepts.name: Regolith and Soil Formation: Weathering as the Foundation of Pedogenesis
key_dimensions: Regolith = all unconsolidated material above bedrock (includes saprolite, transported material, and soil)
Weathering provides parent material for soil; but soil ≠ regolith (soil requires organic matter and biological activity)
Five soil-forming factors (Jenny's CLORPT): Climate, Organisms, Relief, Parent material, Time
UPSC trap: the parent material (regolith) determines mineral nutrient potential of soil, but climate determines the TYPE of weathering and soil order

concepts.name: Climate–Weathering Relationship: Peltier's Morphogenetic Regions
key_dimensions: Peltier (1950) mapped dominant weathering processes against mean annual temperature and precipitation
Strong chemical weathering zone: >1250 mm rainfall, >20°C temperature
Moderate mechanical weathering: 125–250 mm rainfall, −12°C to 2°C (periglacial)
UPSC trap: in Mediterranean climates, BOTH mechanical and chemical weathering operate seasonally — no single dominant type

concepts.name: Mass Wasting as a Weathering-Dependent Process: Classification and Triggers
key_dimensions: Weathering weakens rock/soil cohesion, making it susceptible to mass movement — a direct downstream consequence
Classification: falls (free fall), slides (translational/rotational), flows (debris flow, earthflow, solifluction), creep
Solifluction: slow flow of waterlogged soil over permafrost — unique to periglacial zones, enabled by frost weathering
UPSC trap: creep is the SLOWEST but MOST WIDESPREAD mass movement; often confused with soil erosion — creep requires NO external agent
